# What a GPU KV budget buys: an apples-to-apples study of KV-cache residency policies on one 8 GB consumer GPU

*Draft. Every number in this document is generated from `results/**/metrics.json` by
`scripts/render_docs.py`; the detailed evidence for each claim is in [Findings](FINDINGS.md) and the
per-phase gate reports it links.*

## Abstract

Long-context decoding on a consumer GPU is limited by the KV cache, not the weights. Several
systems keep only part of the cache in VRAM, by eviction, by query-aware selection, or by
offloading to host memory, but they are rarely compared on equal terms, and almost never on the
hardware where the budget actually binds. We build LazyKV, a tiered KV-cache runtime for Hugging
Face Transformers, and use it to measure nine residency policies, from a sliding window with an
attention sink to query-aware block selection over a pinned CPU tier with exact CPU-side attention,
under one budget sweep, one prompt set and one set of quality metrics, on an RTX 5060 Laptop GPU.
At 32,768 tokens with Llama-3.2-1B, no policy that skips KV retains 99%
of the full cache's needle-in-a-haystack accuracy below a full budget: on
300 paired prompts, Quest-style selection fails that bar at a
50% budget (paired 95% CI 94.7%–98.9%)
and sits on it at 75%. Computing the non-resident attention on the CPU and merging it exactly
recovers the full cache's answers at a 6.25%
budget, at 6.2× the decode time. The result
the design did not predict is that, once selection makes transfers small, decode is bound by the
per-layer host round trip that decides what to move, not by moving it: halving the bytes on the
wire made decode slower, a prefetch that hid every copy made it slower, and moving no KV at all was
the slowest rung. We also find that perplexity can show no change where retrieval loses a tenth or
more, that the budget *fraction*, not a constant token budget, is what transfers across context
length, and that at tight budgets query-aware selection loses its lead on multi-hop retrieval. All code,
raw metrics and negative results are public.

## 1. Introduction

A decoding transformer reads every key and value it has cached, for every layer, at every step. At
long context that cache, not the model, is what exhausts an 8 GB GPU. The literature offers three
kinds of answer. *Eviction* drops tokens judged unimportant, by recency with an attention sink
(StreamingLLM) or by accumulated attention (H2O). *Query-aware selection* keeps the cache but attends
only to the blocks that can matter for the current query (Quest). *Offloading* keeps the cache in
host memory and moves what is needed to the GPU, sometimes ahead of time (InfiniGen, ArkVale,
ShadowKV). These systems overlap heavily, are usually evaluated on datacenter GPUs with their own
baselines, and are rarely placed on one frontier.

This paper does not propose a new mechanism. It asks a narrower question, on the hardware where it
matters: *under a fixed GPU KV budget on one consumer GPU, how much retrieval quality does each
residency policy retain, and at what cost?* Our contributions:

1. **An apples-to-apples ladder.** Nine policies, each adding one mechanism to the last, measured
   with the same budget sweep, prompts, kernels and metrics, and shown to be combinable: across the
   phases that measured the same condition, accuracy agrees to within
   0.00 pp (§5.1).
2. **A headline number that cannot be gamed**, resolved as far as the benchmark allows: the smallest
   budget at which a policy keeps 99% of full-cache NIAH accuracy, with paired confidence intervals
   on 300 prompts (§5.1).
3. **A negative systems result.** On this machine, reducing bytes moved over PCIe does not reduce
   decode latency; the cost is a per-layer constant on the host, measured by an ablation that removes
   it while fetching identical blocks (§5.2).
4. **Evidence about the metrics themselves**: perplexity is a poor proxy for retrieval under a
   budget, the budget fraction is the parameterization that transfers across context, and
   needle retrieval overstates query-aware selection relative to multi-hop retrieval (§5.3–5.5).

## 2. Why dense offload is not an option

Decode attention is memory-bandwidth bound. If a block lives in host memory, it must be fetched,
skipped, or attended to where it is. We measured the first option before building anything. On this
laptop, pinned host-to-device copies reach
26.52 GB/s GB/s and device-to-device copies
130.90 GB/s GB/s, a ratio of
4.9×. At 65,536 tokens, fetching one
layer's KV costs 11.5× the GPU attention
it feeds, so prefetching cannot hide it. The viable designs therefore combine *selection* — attend
to a small, query-chosen set of blocks, and move only those — with, optionally, *exact CPU-side
attention* over the rest, merged with the GPU result through the log-sum-exp rescaling that makes
softmax attention associative (FlashAttention, Ring Attention).

## 3. System

LazyKV integrates with Transformers through `Cache` subclasses and one registered attention
function; nothing else is patched.

- **Blocks.** The KV is managed in 64-token blocks. A sweep from 16 to 256 tokens (Phase 4) is a
  trade curve rather than a search for a better default: smaller blocks select more precisely,
  larger ones cut the tier's per-block host work, and no size clears the 99% bar. The first layers
  stay dense; the rest select.
- **Selection (rung 5).** Each block stores the elementwise minimum and maximum of its keys; an
  upper bound on q·k for the block costs O(head dim), and the top-K blocks by bound, plus the sink
  and the newest block, are attended (Quest's criterion).
- **CPU tier (rungs 6–8).** Sealed blocks are written once to pinned host pools. VRAM holds a fixed
  number of slots per KV head; blocks a step selects that are not resident are fetched on demand
  (rung 6), speculatively one layer ahead (rung 7, InfiniGen's insight), or from an int8 warm/cold
  tier (rung 8).
- **Exact merge (rung 9).** Attention over the blocks VRAM does not hold is computed on the CPU from
  a float32 mirror and merged exactly with the GPU's partial result.

The cheaper rungs are GPU-only: a sliding window with an attention sink (rung 2), block LRU (rung 3)
and H2O-style attention-score eviction (rung 4). Rung 1 is the full cache.

## 4. Methodology

**Hardware and software.** One RTX 5060 Laptop GPU (Blackwell, 8 GB), Windows 11, PyTorch with a
CUDA 13 build, a pinned Transformers version. The attention kernel is chosen explicitly and verified
against a float32 reference at startup, because default dispatch on this platform fell to a kernel
33.1× slower than cuDNN at 65,536
tokens, which would have inflated every offloading policy's apparent benefit.

**Model and prompts.** Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct at a pinned revision; Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with 4-bit
weights and bf16 KV as a stress model. Needle-in-a-haystack prompts (single, multi-key and
multi-value needles, five depths) are built from a public-domain novel with a fixed seed, so every
phase sees the same prompts at a given context.

**Budgets.** Every policy gets the same sweep of budget fractions of the full KV (75%, 50%, 25%,
12.5%, 6.25%), at 32,768 tokens for the frontier and at
4 contexts for the context sweep.

**Quality.** The headline is NIAH accuracy as a share of the full cache's (*retention*). Beside it:
teacher-forced KL divergence and top-1 agreement against the full cache, long-document perplexity,
RULER variable tracking, and four LongBench QA subsets. Every quality number carries a bootstrap or
paired confidence interval; paired comparisons use exact sign tests. Because the fast cuDNN decode
kernel is not bit-repeatable for single-query decode, quality is scored on a deterministic kernel.

**Timing.** Conditions are interleaved in random order, repeated over independent runs and reported
as medians with ranges; the process opts out of Windows power throttling after Phase 1 found it
moving the benchmark to efficiency cores at
2.08× the latency.

## 5. Results

### 5.1 The headline, and the frontier

</picture>

| Rung | Policy | Smallest budget retaining >= 99% | Best retention measured | at budget | Resident KV, MiB | Tokens/s there |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | Full GPU KV (reference, exact) | 100% | 100.0% | 100% | 1,028 | 52.3 |
| 2 | Sliding window + attention sink | **none** | 62.5% | 75% | 768 | 51.5 |
| 3 | LRU block eviction | **none** | 29.4% | 75% | 768 | 32.2 |
| 4 | Attention-score eviction (H2O style) | **none** | 92.5% | 75% | 768 | 42.6 |
| 5 | Query-aware block selection (Quest style) | **none** | 98.8% | 75% | 1,028 | 35.9 |
| 6 | CPU tier, synchronous fetch | **none** | 98.8% | 75% | 865 | 18.2 |
| 7 | CPU tier + layer-ahead prefetch | **none** | 98.8% | 75% | 913 | 10.8 |
| 8 | CPU tier, int8 warm/cold | **none** | 98.8% | 75% | 1,078 | 35.4 |
| 9 | CPU tier + exact partial-attention merge | 6.25% | 101.3% | 75% | 1,108 | 8.4 |

No approximating rung clears the 99% bar below a full budget; rungs 5–8 come closest, at
98.8% retention at a
75% budget on
45 prompts. Rerun on 300 paired
prompts under a rule fixed before the run, rung 5 retains
96.9% at 50% (CI entirely below the bar) and
99.0% at 75%
(CI 97.6%–100.2%),
which is as far as NIAH can place it. Teacher-forced KL on
12 paired windows does resolve the ordering NIAH cannot: 50% moves the
distribution further from the full cache than 75% in
12 of 12 windows
(sign test p = 0.0005).

The cheap baselines are not close: the window with a sink tops out at
62.5%, LRU at 29.4% and
H2O-style eviction at 92.5%. Rung 5 alone frees no memory — it
attends to less but keeps every block — which is why the CPU tier exists: rung 6 reproduces rung 5's
answers exactly while holding only the budget in VRAM. Rung 9 is flat at the full cache's accuracy
across the whole memory axis, and pays for it in latency and in a
1,848 MiB host mirror the memory axis does not show.

### 5.2 Bytes moved are not the cost

No attempt to make the tier faster by moving fewer bytes closed its gap to the full cache:

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| Twice the VRAM slots at a 25% budget: on-demand fetches from 2,828 to 295 pairs per token | 17.7 → 18.6 tokens/s |
| Layer-ahead prefetch hiding the copies inside compute | slower than synchronous fetch |
| int8 warm/cold tier, half the bytes on the wire | 1.14× slower |
| Remove the per-layer host sync (replay ablation) | 1.10–1.25× faster: the ceiling |
| Move no KV at all: attend to cold blocks on the CPU | 2.28–4.23× slower than the tier it extends, and exact |

At a 25% budget the tier moves 4.5 MiB per
token, under a millisecond of link time, while choosing what to move costs
20–28 ms.
Each selecting layer must bring its top-K indices to the host before it can issue the fetch, and
the context sweep shows that round trip is a per-layer constant: at least
76% of the selecting rungs' manager cost
sits at zero blocks ranked. The replay ablation, which removes the decision while fetching identical
blocks, bounds what a device-side decision could recover: its fastest decode,
23.8 ms per token, is still slower than the full cache's
18.8 ms. On this machine, a tier narrows the gap to
keeping KV in VRAM and never closes it, at any context measured.

### 5.3 Context length: the fraction is what transfers

Sweeping 4 contexts for rungs 2, 5, 6 and 9 shows
accuracy is set by the budget *fraction*: matched at a fraction, retention spreads
2.7× less across contexts than matched at a
constant number of selected blocks, the parameterization Quest uses. A constant token budget
therefore does not carry from one context to another.

### 5.4 Perplexity misses the loss

At 32,768 tokens,
9 of
20 conditions lose at least a tenth of NIAH
retrieval while their perplexity interval includes no change; the window with a sink at a
25% budget keeps
24.4% of retrieval at a perplexity ratio
of 1.024. Perplexity ranks conditions roughly
correctly (Spearman 0.94) but averages the
few tokens that need distant context in with the many that do not, the failure LongPPL describes.

### 5.5 Beyond single needles, and a larger model

On RULER variable tracking, where the question names only the first link of a chain, Quest-style
selection at 6.25% retains
41.5% against the single needle's
61.3% with disjoint intervals
(150 prompts per task), and its lead over the
cheap baselines disappears: it is the best approximating family *for retrieval the query can see*.
On four LongBench subsets no multi-hop shortfall was detected (multi-hop F1 retention
77.2% against
78.6%), but the difference interval
(-21.1 pp to +16.6 pp)
is too wide to exclude the RULER gap. On Llama-3.2-3B at
16,384 tokens, Quest-style selection at 6.25% retains
76.7% of full-cache accuracy against the
1B's 42.9% on the same prompts, while the
window shows no detected model difference; the 1B's tight-budget losses look conservative rather
than a floor. That is one additional model, not a trend.

## 6. Related work

Query-aware block selection with per-block key bounds is Quest (arXiv 2406.10774). Layer-ahead
speculative prefetch from the previous layer's hidden state is InfiniGen (arXiv 2406.19707).
Recallable eviction to host memory is ArkVale (NeurIPS 2024); ShadowKV (arXiv 2410.21465) keeps a
low-rank key cache on the GPU and values on the host. Eviction baselines are StreamingLLM's attention
sink (arXiv 2309.17453), H2O (arXiv 2306.14048) and SnapKV (arXiv 2404.14469). FlexGen
(arXiv 2303.06865) offloads for throughput on one GPU; PagedAttention (arXiv 2309.06180) and LMCache
(arXiv 2510.09665) manage KV for serving. The exact merge relies on the rescaling used by
FlashAttention (arXiv 2205.14135) and Ring Attention (arXiv 2310.01889). Quantized KV caches include
KIVI (arXiv 2402.02750) and KVQuant (arXiv 2401.18079). Benchmarks are RULER (arXiv 2404.06654) and
LongBench (arXiv 2308.14508); LongPPL (arXiv 2410.23771) documents perplexity's blindness to
long-range tokens. The survey behind this section, with what LazyKV does differently from each, is
[Related work](RELATED_WORK.md).

## 7. Limitations

Most results are for one 1B model, on needle retrieval, at one context, with
45 prompts per condition; only rung 5 at 50% and 75% was rerun on
300. The 3B model ran at one context, with 4-bit weights,
because its full reference cache is what did not fit. Prefill is not tiered, so peak VRAM during
prefill is the full KV. Rung 9 is exact in the algebra, not in the bits (bf16 on the GPU, float32
on the CPU). All latency is from one laptop, controlled for by interleaving and repetition rather
than eliminated. The latency conclusion is specific to a platform where the host round trip is
expensive and PCIe is comparatively fast; it should be retested on others before it is generalized.
The full list is [Findings §7](FINDINGS.md#7-limitations).

## 8. Conclusion

On one 8 GB consumer GPU, the last percent of retrieval accuracy cannot be bought by *skipping* KV at
any budget this study measured, and can be bought by *computing* it elsewhere, at a price in latency
and host RAM. Among the approximate policies, query-aware selection is the clear best for retrieval
the query can see, and the CPU tier turns its attention budget into a memory budget without changing
a single answer. What the tier cannot do on this machine is be fast: once selection makes transfers
small, the decision about what to transfer is the cost. We release the runtime, every raw metric and
the negative results, so that the same ladder can be run on other hardware.

## Reproducibility

Code, configs, raw `metrics.json` for every reported run, and the renderer that generates this
document are at <https://github.com/PS12007/LazyKV>. Each phase's gate report lists the commit and
command that produced its numbers.
